claims.text: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction can track time-resolved phase transformations during high-temperature oxidation.
HTXRD can elucidate elemental redistribution specifically within nanoprecipitates of AM-processed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
Time-resolved phase transformations can be correlated with protective or degradative oxide formation.
The AM-processed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a dual-nanoprecipitation microstructure.
The alloy should be exposed to high-temperature oxidation in a controlled atmosphere and under controlled temperature ramping.
Oxidation between approximately 700 and 1000 °C in a controlled atmosphere can mimic service conditions.
Nanoprecipitates in the target alloy may undergo oxidation-induced elemental redistribution.
Nanoprecipitates in the target alloy may undergo oxidation-induced phase transformations.
Distinct nanoprecipitate phases may preferentially oxidize or dissolve during high-temperature oxidation.
Preferential oxidation can produce new oxide phases and deplete associated elements from the alloy.
In situ HTXRD enables continuous identification of time- and temperature-dependent phase formation or transformation.
Elemental redistribution within nanoprecipitates influences the overall oxidation behavior of the target alloy.
HTXRD will detect sequential phase transformations and the emergence of oxide diffraction peaks during oxidation of the target alloy.
Al2O3 peaks may emerge during oxidation of AM-processed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The observed phase evolution will correlate with oxidation kinetics.
HTXRD alone can provide evidence of elemental depletion or enrichment localized within nanoprecipitates.
Linking nanoprecipitate evolution to oxide formation would substantiate improved high-temperature performance.
Cast or wrought counterparts lack the additional strengthening observed in the AM-processed alloy.
Cast or wrought counterparts do not exhibit the distinct nanoprecipitate oxidation behavior attributed to the AM-processed alloy.
Complementary TEM-EDS is required to identify element-specific redistribution within individual nanoprecipitates precisely.
